Lately, I've been revisiting my
[earlier](https://dieghernan.github.io/202210_tidyterra-hillshade/)
[posts](https://dieghernan.github.io/202212_tidyterra-hillshade-2/) on
hillshading and the [tidyterra
FAQs](https://dieghernan.github.io/tidyterra/articles/faqs.html). I wanted to
understand why two maps made from the same digital elevation model (DEM)
could look so different. How much of that comes from the hillshade, and how
much from the way we combine it with the elevation colors?

I started with the [alpha
hack](https://timogrossenbacher.ch/bivariate-maps-with-ggplot2-and-sf/) I used
in my earlier maps. While working on the **tidyterra** FAQs, I discovered
`metR::geom_relief()` and gave it a try. To my surprise, I liked the **metR**
map better!

## Data and setup

<!-- TODO: Restore the elevation tile zoom to 8 before publishing. -->

In this post, I'm using a DEM for the area around the Strait of
Gibraltar in southern Spain. I get the boundary from **mapSpain** and use its
bounding box to download the elevation tiles at zoom level 7 with **elevatr**.
Then I reproject the DEM to match the boundary. All the maps use that same DEM,
and every color map uses **tidyterra**'s `etopo1` elevation palette.

The terrain tiles include elevations on land and depths below sea level, so the
map also shows the seabed around the Strait.

```{r}
#| label: setup-and-elevation-data

library(terra)
library(mapSpain)
library(elevatr)
library(metR)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyterra)
library(ggblend)

map_family <- "inter-tight"
sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter Tight", family = map_family)
showtext::showtext_opts(dpi = knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi"))
showtext::showtext_auto()

map_background <- "#faf8f2"
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_family = map_family) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = map_background, colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = map_background, colour = NA),
      plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#203b47"),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = "#203b47"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.key = element_rect(fill = map_background, colour = NA),
      legend.spacing.x = unit(0, "pt")
    )
)

# The data

# Use Andalusia and Melilla to get the bbox.
the_strait <- esp_get_ccaa(c("Andalucia", "Melilla"), epsg = 3857)

# Create the cache directory if needed.

if (!dir.exists(tools::R_user_dir("elevatr", "cache"))) {
  dir.create(tools::R_user_dir("elevatr", "cache"), recursive = TRUE, )
}

dem <- get_elev_raster(
  the_strait,
  z = 7,
  clip = "bbox",
  tmp_dir = tools::R_user_dir("elevatr", "cache")
) |>
  rast()

dem <- project(dem, pull_crs(the_strait))
names(dem) <- "elevation"
```

## Hillshade with the alpha hack

For my first try, I followed the example in the **terra** help. It calculates
slope and aspect from the DEM, creates a hillshade with a single
light direction and draws a semi-transparent elevation layer on top. I do the
same in **ggplot2** and set the elevation colors to 40% opacity with
`alpha = 0.4`.

I set the sun 40° above the horizon, with light coming from the west (270°). For
the alpha hack, I draw the hillshade in grayscale, then extract the colors with
`layer_data()` and pass those colors directly to the hillshade layer. That
leaves the `fill` scale free for the elevation palette and its legend.

```{r}
#| label: single-direction-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Grayscale relief map of the Strait of Gibraltar. West-facing slopes catch the light,
#|   outlining ridges in the east while the Guadalquivir lowlands stay
#|   mostly smooth.

slope_1 <- terrain(dem, "slope", unit = "radians")
aspect_1 <- terrain(dem, "aspect", unit = "radians")

# Single shadow
hill_1 <- shade(slope_1, aspect_1, 40, direction = 270)

pal_greys <- hcl.colors(1000, "Grays")

gghill_1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_1, maxcell = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = pal_greys, na.value = NA) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Single-direction hillshade", x = NULL, y = NULL)

# Show

print(gghill_1)

# Get colors

pal_1 <- layer_data(gghill_1) |> dplyr::pull(fill)

plot_brks <- seq(-2500, 3500, by = 500)
elevation_legend <- guide_legend(
  title = "Elevation (m)",
  direction = "horizontal",
  nrow = 1,
  keywidth = unit(0.38, "in"),
  keyheight = unit(0.14, "in"),
  theme = theme(
    legend.text.position = "bottom",
    legend.title.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.key.spacing.x = unit(2, "pt")
  ),
  override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: transparent-color-overlay
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map with muted greens in the lowlands, ochres in the mountains
#|   and blue offshore. The west-lit ridges show through the pale colors.

map_alpha <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_1, fill = pal_1, maxcell = Inf) +
  geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf) +
  scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
    "etopo1",
    alpha = 0.4,
    breaks = plot_brks,
    labels = scales::label_comma()
  ) +
  guides(alpha = "none", fill = elevation_legend) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Transparent color overlay", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(map_alpha)
```

## Shaded relief with metR

Enter **metR**. This is the approach I tried in the **tidyterra** FAQs using
`metR::geom_relief()`. Here I draw the hillshade directly from the DEM
and draw the elevation colors on top. This time I map `alpha` to elevation,
so more of the hillshade shows through in the mountains.

```{r}
#| label: metr-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   High-contrast grayscale relief map. Alternating dark and light slopes
#|   define the eastern mountains and trace ridges on the seabed south of
#|   the coast.

hill_metr <- ggplot(dem, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_relief(aes(z = elevation)) +
  coord_sf(crs = terra::crs(dem), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Hillshade with metR", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(hill_metr)
```

```{r}
#| label: metr-relief-map
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map with pale ochre mountains, green lowlands and blue water.
#|   High-contrast shading is most visible in the eastern ranges, where the
#|   elevation colors are more transparent.

map_metr <- ggplot(dem, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_relief(aes(z = elevation)) +
  geom_spatraster(
    data = dem,
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    aes(alpha = after_stat(value)),
    maxcell = Inf
  ) +
  scale_alpha(range = c(1, 0.25)) +
  scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
    "etopo1",
    breaks = plot_brks,
    labels = scales::label_comma()
  ) +
  guides(alpha = "none", fill = elevation_legend) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Elevation-dependent transparency", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(map_metr)
```

This is the point where I started preferring the **metR** map. Look at the
mountains in the east! The ridges stand out more clearly, and the colors look
less washed out.

Could I get a similar result by changing how I combined the hillshade and the
elevation colors?

## Introducing ggblend

[Barney Harris](https://barney.fly.dev/2026/01/27/ggplot2-blending-adventure/)
had noticed a similar problem in the first version of my Romania map. He used
the multiply blend mode in **ggblend** to combine the two layers.

I went back to the hillshade and elevation palette from the first map and
switched from the alpha hack to `ggblend::blend("multiply")`. Let's see how it
looks.

```{r}
#| label: multiply-single-direction-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map with deeper greens and blues than the transparent overlay.
#|   Dark slopes add texture to the ochre mountains while the western
#|   lowlands remain mostly smooth.

map_multiply <- ggplot() +
  list(
    geom_spatraster(data = hill_1, fill = pal_1, maxcell = Inf),
    geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf),
    scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
      "etopo1",
      breaks = plot_brks,
      labels = scales::label_comma()
    )
  ) |>
  blend("multiply") +
  guides(alpha = "none", fill = elevation_legend) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Multiply blend", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(map_multiply)
```

The colors looked better, but I still wanted to see what a single light
direction was missing.

## Enhancing the hillshading

So far, my **terra** hillshade has used a single light source from the west.
[Dominic
Royé](https://dominicroye.github.io/blog/hillshade-effect/#multidirectional-shadows)
shows what happens when you light the terrain from four directions. He keeps the
sun at the same angle above the horizon and adds the four hillshades together.

So let's add multidirectional shadows to our map. I'll keep the multiply blend
and the light 40° above the horizon. Royé sums his four hillshades. I average
mine (225°, 270°, 315° and 360°) to keep the values on the same scale as a
single hillshade.

```{r}
#| label: multidirectional-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Grayscale relief map. Highlights pick out ridges running in several
#|   directions across the eastern mountains, with softer shadows on
#|   adjacent slopes.

hill_2 <- shade(slope_1, aspect_1, 40, direction = c(225, 270, 315, 360)) |>
  mean()

gghill_2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_2, maxcell = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = pal_greys, na.value = NA) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Multidirectional hillshade", x = NULL, y = NULL)

# Show
print(gghill_2)

# Get colors
pal_2 <- layer_data(gghill_2) |> dplyr::pull(fill)
```

```{r}
#| label: multiply-multidirectional-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map with textured ochre mountain ridges, deep green lowlands in
#|   the west and blue offshore areas where the seabed texture remains
#|   visible.

map_multi <- ggplot() +
  list(
    geom_spatraster(data = hill_2, fill = pal_2, maxcell = Inf),
    geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf),
    scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
      "etopo1",
      breaks = plot_brks,
      labels = scales::label_comma()
    )
  ) |>
  blend("multiply") +
  guides(alpha = "none", fill = elevation_legend) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Multidirectional multiply blend", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(map_multi)
```

Better, but I still preferred the **metR** map. What was going on?

## Jackpot! Stretching the hillshade

An earlier experiment comparing **metR** and **terra** on Swiss elevation data
gave me one more idea to try. The calculation behind `geom_relief()` produces
shade values between 0 and 1, as I explain in [the bonus section](#bonus-recreating-metrs-relief-shading-from-scratch).
In that experiment, the **terra** values covered a narrower range.

**What if I stretch the hillshade before blending it with the elevation
colors?**

I map the 5th percentile of the multidirectional hillshade to 0 and the 95th
to 1. Values in between are rescaled linearly, and anything beyond those
percentiles is clipped to 0 or 1.

This is a visual adjustment, not a new hillshading method. It increases contrast
and makes subtle terrain features easier to see, but it does not add any terrain
information.

I also wanted a brighter result, closer to the **metR** map. Let's see what
happens when I stretch the hillshade and use a lighter grayscale ramp.

```{r}
#| label: stretch-multidirectional-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Grayscale relief map with a pale background and sharper gray shadows
#|   along the eastern mountain ridges and the slopes of the seabed.

# Stretching
q <- as.numeric(quantile(values(hill_2), c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE))

hill_3 <- clamp((hill_2 - q[1]) / diff(q), 0, 1)

gghill_3 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_3, maxcell = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    high = "white",
    low = "gray80",
    na.value = "transparent"
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Stretched multidirectional hillshade", x = NULL, y = NULL)

# Show
print(gghill_3)

# Get colors
pal_3 <- layer_data(gghill_3) |> dplyr::pull(fill)
```

And now let's check the result:

```{r}
#| label: final-map-with-stretched-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map of the Strait of Gibraltar with bright blue bathymetry, green
#|   lowlands and ochre mountains. Fine shadows define the eastern ridges and
#|   the seabed.

map_final <- ggplot() +
  list(
    geom_spatraster(data = hill_3, fill = pal_3, maxcell = Inf),
    geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf),
    scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
      "etopo1",
      breaks = plot_brks,
      labels = scales::label_comma()
    )
  ) |>
  blend("multiply") +
  guides(alpha = "none", fill = elevation_legend) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Stretched hillshade with multiply", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(map_final)
```

The devil is in the details. Here's the same part of Sierra Nevada with **metR**
alongside three versions of the multiply blend. The last panel shows the
combined effect of the stretch and the lighter gray ramp.

```{r}
#| label: sierra-nevada-detail
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.25
#| fig-crop: false
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Four close-ups of Sierra Nevada in a two-by-two grid. The top row shows
#|   metR and the west-lit multiply blend. The bottom row shows the
#|   multidirectional and stretched versions. The last panel is brighter,
#|   with fine ridges visible across the mountain range.

sierra_nevada <- sf::st_bbox(
  c(xmin = -3.75, ymin = 36.83, xmax = -2.75, ymax = 37.34),
  crs = sf::st_crs(4326)
) |>
  sf::st_as_sfc() |>
  sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(terra::crs(dem))) |>
  sf::st_bbox()

sierra_view <- coord_sf(
  xlim = unname(sierra_nevada[c("xmin", "xmax")]),
  ylim = unname(sierra_nevada[c("ymin", "ymax")]),
  expand = FALSE,
  datum = NA
)
detail_theme <- theme(
  legend.position = "none",
  plot.margin = margin(4, 5, 4, 5)
)

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::grid.rect(gp = grid::gpar(fill = map_background, col = NA))
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(
  width = 0.97,
  height = 0.97,
  layout = grid::grid.layout(2, 2)
))
print(
  map_metr + sierra_view + detail_theme + labs(title = "metR"),
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1)
)
print(
  map_multiply + sierra_view + detail_theme + labs(title = "West light"),
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 2)
)
print(
  map_multi + sierra_view + detail_theme + labs(title = "Four directions"),
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 1)
)
print(
  map_final + sierra_view + detail_theme + labs(title = "Stretched hillshade"),
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 2)
)
grid::popViewport()
```

## Comparing the maps

Each row pairs a hillshade with its color map. The first and third rows share
the same hillshade, so you can compare transparency with multiply blending.

```{r}
#| label: hillshade-comparison-poster
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 19
#| fig-crop: false
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Five rows pair grayscale hillshades with colored elevation maps. The
#|   first and third rows share a hillshade, and multiply blending in the
#|   third row gives deeper colors. The metR row has the strongest grayscale
#|   contrast. The last row brings out fine ridges on a brighter map.

elevation_guide <- ggplotGrob(map_final)
elevation_guide <- elevation_guide$grobs[[
  match("guide-box-bottom", elevation_guide$layout$name)
]]

poster_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_blank(),
  legend.position = "none",
  plot.margin = margin(5, 8, 5, 8)
)
heading_style <- grid::gpar(
  fontfamily = map_family,
  fontface = "bold",
  fontsize = 14,
  col = "#203b47"
)

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::grid.rect(gp = grid::gpar(fill = map_background, col = NA))
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(
  width = 0.97,
  height = 0.97,
  layout = grid::grid.layout(
    8,
    3,
    widths = grid::unit(c(0.16, 1, 1), "null"),
    heights = grid::unit(c(0.31, 0.18, rep(1, 5), 0.3), "null")
  )
))

grid::grid.text(
  "Five ways to shade the Strait of Gibraltar",
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1:3),
  gp = grid::gpar(
    fontfamily = map_family, fontface = "bold", fontsize = 24, col = "#203b47"
  )
)
grid::grid.text(

grid::grid.text(

)
print(gghill_1 + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 3, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(map_alpha + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 3, layout.pos.col = 3))

grid::grid.text(
  "metR",
  rot = 90,
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 4, layout.pos.col = 1),
  gp = heading_style
)
print(hill_metr + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 4, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(map_metr + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 4, layout.pos.col = 3))

grid::grid.text(
  "Multiply",
  rot = 90,
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 5, layout.pos.col = 1),
  gp = heading_style
)
print(gghill_1 + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 5, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(map_multiply + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 5, layout.pos.col = 3))

grid::grid.text(
  "Multidirectional",
  rot = 90,
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 6, layout.pos.col = 1),
  gp = heading_style
)
print(gghill_2 + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 6, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(map_multi + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 6, layout.pos.col = 3))

grid::grid.text(
  "Stretched",
  rot = 90,
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 7, layout.pos.col = 1),

print(map_final + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 7, layout.pos.col = 3))

```

Look at the coast in the first and third rows. With multiply, the greens along
the coast and the blues offshore are stronger, even though both maps use the
same hillshade. In the last row, the stretch and lighter gray ramp give the
seabed a brighter look, and I can still pick out its ridges. That's the version
I'd use for this map.

## Bonus: Recreating metR’s relief shading from scratch

The stretched hillshade got me closer to the look I liked in the **metR** map.
But I still wanted to know what `geom_relief()` was doing differently. So I
took a look under the hood. Conventional hillshading uses both slope and
aspect. [The **metR** calculation](https://github.com/eliocamp/metR/blob/main/R/geom_relief.R)
uses just the downhill direction. A gentle slope and a steep slope facing the
same way can get exactly the same shade.

$$
I = \frac{1 + \cos(\theta - \alpha)}{2}
$$

Here $$\theta$$ is the downhill angle, computed with `atan2(-dy, -dx)`, and
$$\alpha$$ is the light direction, converted to radians from `sun.angle + 90`.
At `sun.angle = 0`, slopes that descend toward the north get the brightest
shade. Positive angles turn the light counterclockwise. The cosine gives an
intensity from 0 to 1.

I can get the same calculation on a regular grid with base **R** and
**terra**. I use three-point differences, centered in the interior and
one-sided at the edges. Raster rows run north to south, so the vertical
step is negative. This loads the raster into memory and needs at least three
rows and columns. I keep the original CRS and prefer a projected grid so both
axes measure distance in the same units.

```{r}
#| label: relief-function

relief <- function(x, sun.angle = 60) {
  stopifnot(
    inherits(x, "SpatRaster"), terra::nlyr(x) == 1L,
    nrow(x) >= 3L, ncol(x) >= 3L
  )
  z <- terra::as.matrix(x, wide = TRUE)
  spacing <- terra::res(x)

  deriv <- function(z, h) {
    n <- length(z)
    c(
      (-3 * z[1] + 4 * z[2] - z[3]) / (2 * h),
      (z[3:n] - z[1:(n - 2)]) / (2 * h),
      (3 * z[n] - 4 * z[n - 1] + z[n - 2]) / (2 * h)
    )
  }

  dx <- t(apply(z, 1, deriv, h = spacing[1]))
  dy <- apply(z, 2, deriv, h = -spacing[2])
  angle <- (sun.angle + 90) * pi / 180
  shade <- (1 + cos(atan2(-dy, -dx) - angle)) / 2
  shade[is.na(z)] <- NA_real_

  out <- terra::rast(x)
  terra::values(out) <- as.vector(t(shade))
  names(out) <- "relief"
  out
}
```

Here are the two versions side by side. Both use the same DEM, map extent and
light direction (`sun.angle = 60`), with intensities from 0 to 1 mapped to
the same gray20-to-white ramp.

```{r}
#| label: recreated-metr-relief
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-crop: false
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Two grayscale maps of the Strait of Gibraltar compare metR with a
#|   base R and terra recreation. Both show similar bands of light and dark
#|   on mountain ridges and across the seabed.

light_direction <- 60
dark <- "gray20"
light <- "white"
hill_recreated <- relief(dem, sun.angle = light_direction)

map_view <- coord_sf(
  crs = terra::crs(dem),
  xlim = c(xmin(dem), xmax(dem)),
  ylim = c(ymin(dem), ymax(dem)),
  expand = FALSE
)

relief_metr <- ggplot(dem, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_relief(
    aes(z = elevation),
    sun.angle = light_direction, dark = dark, light = light,
    interpolate = FALSE
  ) +
  map_view +
  labs(title = "metR", x = NULL, y = NULL)

relief_terra <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(
    data = hill_recreated, maxcell = Inf, interpolate = FALSE,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = dark, high = light, limits = c(0, 1), na.value = NA) +
  map_view +
  labs(title = "Base R and terra", x = NULL, y = NULL)

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::grid.rect(gp = grid::gpar(fill = map_background, col = NA))
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(
  width = 0.97,
  height = 0.97,
  layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 2)
))
print(relief_metr, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.col = 1))
print(relief_terra, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.col = 2))
grid::popViewport()
```

The intensities matched
on a complete test grid with equally scaled axes. **metR** takes derivatives
after **ggplot2** transforms the coordinates, so scaling the axes differently
can change the result. I use the raster coordinates. The centered difference
skips the center cell, so I explicitly keep missing elevations blank. Gaps
can also leave neighboring cells unshaded, while **metR** can calculate
across them.

## What I learned

For me, **how we display a hillshade can matter just as much as how we
calculate it**.

Overlaying semi-transparent elevation colors works, but blending modes give us
more control over how the colors and hillshade interact.

Multidirectional hillshading can reveal terrain features that might be less
visible with a single light source. However, it doesn't necessarily produce a
better-looking map.

For the map I'd use here, stretching the hillshade was the missing piece.
By expanding its tonal range, we can bring out subtle terrain features without
changing the underlying elevation data or the hillshading algorithm.
